newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OSCE Albania envoy says still no date for visit.
newsitem.headline: OSCE Albania envoy says still no date for visit.

text.p: Franz Vranitzky, special envoy to Albania for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said on Thursday the exact timing of his planned fact-finding visit to the troubled Balkan state remained open.

"I have had a telephone conversation with President Sali Berisha and we agreed that the OSCE mission will take place at the earliest possible moment. We have agreed to stay in contact," Vranitzky told a news conference at OSCE headquarters in Vienna.

The 54-member OSCE, Europe's top security body, on Tuesday appointed former Austrian chancellor Vranitzky to travel to Albania and assess the situation in the troubled nation, where a state of emergency has been declared.
On Wednesday, however, Albanian officials had informed the OSCE that the visit "was not welcome", Vranitzky said, adding that he still expected to travel to Tirana "in the next few days".

More than 20 people have been reported killed in Albania's south in violent protests, sparked by the collapse of several get-rich-quick investment schemes. A night-time curfew has been ordered and troops have been called in to quell the unrest.
"Our basic aim is to offer help," Vranitzky said. "I have no illusion that the mission is not going to be a very difficult one."
But the 59-year old Social Democrat said the West needed to take urgent action to prevent the crisis in Albania, Europe's poorest country, from spiralling out of control.
"Politically, the aim is that the OSCE has to take action at a very early stage to prevent a second Balkan catastrophe, after the long-sought and hard-won solution in Bosnia."

Vranitzky said he had been instructed to seek dialogue with all political forces in the country, but declined to speculate on the outcome of his mission. "I will refrain from any premature euphoria about its success," he said.

Vranitzky added that Berisha had told him during a long phone conversation on Thursday morning that the situation in Albania was "very serious", but that he had no intention of stepping up military action to quash unrest in the south.
"The president said that he did not have the intention to intensify military (actions). But from here, it is of course hard to judge what is really going on in the south," he said.
The OSCE Troika of Swiss, Danish and Polish foreign ministers was expected to travel to Tirana on Thursday to prepare Vranitzky's visit.

A delegation from the Council of Europe, which promotes democracy and human rights, is already in Albania, and a European Union mission headed by the Dutch foreign minister is due to arrive there on Friday.

The OSCE instructed Vranitzky to assure Berisha's government of its readiness to assist in resolving the crisis that has engulfed the country, "possibly in cooperation with other relevant international organisations".
"The most important goal is to make clear to the Albanians that we come not as enemies, but as members of a group which they also belong to," Vranitzky said.
